title: How Your Memory Really Works
desc: You try to remember what you had for dinner last Tuesday, and the answer doesn't arrive like a video. It's built, piece by piece, from clues. In this calm, sourced deep dive we follow one ordinary memory from the first second it forms to the day it changes and fades: why most of what you see and hear is gone in moments, why a tiny workspace holds only a few things, what Henry Molaison's case taught us, what your brain replays while you sleep, where a memory actually lives, why a word can sit on the tip of your tongue, what a forgetting curve looks like, why remembering is rebuilding, and why a vivid memory can feel certain and still be wrong. Every claim comes from named studies, with the doubts left in. At the end there is a slow, gentle wind-down, so you can listen until you drift off.
plan: b01: hook (what did you have for dinner last Tuesday) + 'Tonight, we'll explore' list + the journey of one memory in five stops; no filing cabinet (Azevedo et al. 2009, ~86 billion neurons; Bartlett 1932 quote; Schacter & Addis 2007); photographic memory myth (Stromeyer & Psotka 1970); open loop: how a vivid memory can feel certain and be wrong (paid off b14)

b02: getting in: Atkinson & Shiffrin 1968; Sperling 1960 partial report; echoic memory (Darwin, Turvey & Crowder 1972); Cherry 1953 and Moray 1959; attention as the gate; pictures stick (Brady et al. 2008, Standing 1973)

b03: working memory: Peterson & Peterson 1959 and Keppel & Underwood 1962; Miller 1956 and Cowan 2001; Chase & Simon 1973 chess; Ericsson, Chase & Faloon 1980 (79 digits); Baddeley & Hitch 1974; serial position (Murdock 1962, Glanzer & Cunitz 1966)

b04: what decides what stays: levels of processing (Craik & Lockhart 1972, Craik & Tulving 1975); the penny (Nickerson & Adams 1979) and the Apple logo (Blake, Nazarian & Castel 2015); von Restorff 1933; self-reference (Rogers et al. 1977); generation effect (Slamecka & Graf 1978); emotion (Cahill et al. 1994); photos (Henkel 2014) and the Google effect (Sparrow et al. 2011, not replicated)

b05: staying: H.M. (Scoville & Milner 1957; Milner, Corkin 1968 mirror drawing); two kinds of memory; consolidation (Muller & Pilzecker 1900; Ribot 1881; Squire); Annese et al. 2014 brain atlas; amnesia at the movies (Baxendale 2004); taxi drivers (Maguire et al. 2000, Woollett & Maguire 2011)

b06: the night shift: Jenkins & Dallenbach 1924; Wilson & McNaughton 1994 replay; Ji & Wilson 2007; Diekelmann & Born 2010; Rasch et al. 2007 rose scent; Yoo et al. 2007; Walker et al. 2002 finger tapping; Mednick et al. 2003 naps; Wagner et al. 2004 insight

b07: where memories live: Semon 1904, Lashley 1950; Hebb 1949; Bliss & Lomo 1973; Kandel (Aplysia, Nobel 2000); Liu et al. 2012 and Ramirez et al. 2013 (mouse engrams); Quiroga et al. 2005; place and grid cells (O'Keefe & Dostrovsky 1971, Hafting et al. 2005)

b08: kinds of memory: Ryle 1949; Tulving 1972; Squire's map; Clive Wearing (Deborah Wearing, Forever Today); Warrington & Weiskrantz 1970 priming; source amnesia (Schacter et al. 1984); Knowlton et al. 1996 habit learning; prospective memory (Einstein & McDaniel 1990) and implementation intentions (Gollwitzer 1999)

b09: coming back: Tulving & Pearlstone 1966; Tulving & Thomson 1973; Godden & Baddeley 1975 divers, Saufley et al. 1985 and Smith & Vela 2001 caveats; Proust, Herz & Schooler 2002, Chu & Downes 2000; Janata et al. 2007 music; Eich & Metcalfe 1989 mood; Brown & McNeill 1966 tip of the tongue

b10: fading: Ebbinghaus 1885, Murre & Dros 2015; spacing (Cepeda et al. 2006); testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke 2006, Karpicke & Roediger 2008); Kornell & Bjork 2008 desirable difficulties; Bahrick 1984 permastore

b11: forgetting as a feature: Luria 1968 (S., Shereshevsky); Parker et al. 2006 and Patihis et al. 2013 (HSAM); Anderson, Bjork & Bjork 1994; Anderson & Green 2001; Richards & Frankland 2017; Schacter's seven sins (1999)
b12: changing: Bartlett 1932 and Bergman & Roediger 1999; Brewer & Treyens 1981; Roediger & McDermott 1995; Loftus & Pickrell 1995; Gabbert et al. 2003 memory conformity

b13: reconsolidation: Misanin et al. 1968; Nader, Schafe & LeDoux 2000; Schiller et al. 2010 and the 2020 registered replication; Kindt et al. 2009; Bouton 2004; Hupbach et al. 2007; Tversky & Marsh 2000

b14: certainty: Brown & Kulik 1977; Neisser & Harsch 1992; Talarico & Rubin 2003; Hirst et al. 2015; Johnson & Raye 1981; Garry et al. 1996 imagination inflation; Wells & Bradfield 1998; Wixted & Wells 2017; weapon focus (Loftus et al. 1987); own-race bias

b15: a whole life: Conway & Pleydell-Pearce 2000; childhood amnesia (Freud, Josselyn & Frankland 2012, Akers et al. 2014); reminiscence bump (Rubin et al. 1998; Berntsen & Rubin 2004); fading affect bias (Walker et al. 2003) and rosy retrospection (Mitchell et al. 1997); callback to Tuesday's dinner; recap

b16: training a memory: method of loci (Cicero; Maguire et al. 2003; Dresler et al. 2017); brain training (Owen et al. 2010; Simons et al. 2016); exercise (Erickson et al. 2011); production effect (MacLeod et al. 2010); handwriting vs laptops (Mueller & Oppenheimer 2014, smaller in replications)

b17: guided wind-down: Tetris images at sleep onset (Stickgold et al. 2000), a slow walk through a familiar house, the breath, letting the day settle, goodnight, end segment teasing 'How Motivation Really Works'
